The Tārā Tantra
First Chapter.
Oṃ, homage to Tāriṇī.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, the goddess Bhairavī, having rested comfortably upon her bed, questioned Maheśvara, the God of gods. (1.1)
O Lord of Gods! O Master! Tell me how those two, Kulabhairava and Buddha-vaśiṣṭha, who were mentioned previously, attained perfection through that mantra.
Bhairava said:
Kṣa alone is the supreme deity, Janārdana in the form of Buddha; and having fully recited the five-syllabled great mantra of Ugratārā. (1.3)
The performer of acts such as creation attained freedom from old age and death;
Vasiṣṭha also, having propitiated him, reached the world of the stars.
O Beloved! Having become a master of the perfections of yoga, he shines even today.
I shall now declare the doctrine of its extraction, by which one becomes the Lord of All. (1.5)
Having first extracted the Praṇava, [followed by] Hṛllekhā, Kulakāminī, Kūrca, and Astra—this king of mantras is like another celestial tree. (1.6)
By propitiating Him alone, Sadāśiva became the Lord of All;
likewise did the sages Durvāsas, Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Bhāradvāja, and others. (1.7)
Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the others were victorious Kṣatriyas;
thus, O Goddess, has this most excellent secret been told to you. 1/8.
This must be guarded with great effort if you have any affection for me. (1.9)
Bhairavī said: "O Lord! By your grace, I have heard the mantra which is like a celestial tree;
now tell me the morning ritual that was performed by the Buddha."
Bhairava said:
I shall now declare the morning rites by which a man becomes a perfected one (siddha);
during the latter part of the forenoon, the practitioner [should meditate] upon the thousand-petaled lotus.
Upon the pedestal situated within the pericarp, in the vicinity of the lunar disc,
[he was] resembling pure crystal and resplendent with a pure silken garment.
He displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; he is peaceful, with a serene face and eyes;
he is richly adorned with perfumes, flowers, and ornaments; and his mind is intent upon his beloved. (1.13)
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Guru with mental offerings such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth;
then one should recite the mantra three times, seven times, or even ten times. (1.14)
Having first uttered the Vāgbhava [syllable], [one says] the name of the Guru and his beloved;
"I worship the Śrīpādukā, obeisance"—this mantra is dear to the Guru. (1.15)
Having offered [the oblation] with the Guhyātimantra, the mantra-practitioner should perform the hymn of praise.
Oṃ, homage to you, O Blessed Lord, Protector! To Śiva in the form of the Guru, who has assumed manifold forms for the sake of perfectly accomplishing the descent of knowledge. (1.17)
Salutations to You, who exist as existence itself, whose form is existence, whose nature is that of the Supreme Self,
who are the sun that dispels the darkness of all ignorance, and who are composed of pure consciousness.

To the one who is independent, whose form is anointed with compassion, whose essence is Śiva; to the one who is dependent upon his devotees, bestowing prosperity upon those who are fortunate. || 1/19 ||

For the sake of discernment for the discerning, for the sake of investigation for the investigative, for the sake of illumination for the illuminating—to the one whose very form is knowledge for the wise. (1.20)
Having offered praise with the mantra beginning with "ajñāna," one should perform a prostration.
[One should meditate] upon Kulakuṇḍalī in the Mūlādhāra, whose nature is that of the Root-Vidyā. (1.21)
Resembling ten million suns in brilliance, yet as slender as a strand of a lotus fiber.
Having fashioned it in the form of a sleeping serpent and endowed with three and a half coils,
one should then infuse it with consciousness by means of the *haṃsa* mantra.
Having split the six lotuses, one should bring [the energy] down to the base of the pericarp;
then, O Mistress of the Kula, one should remember these Kaula gurus. (1.24)
The one named Prahlādānandanātha, Sanakānanda, Kumārānandanātha, and Vasiṣṭhānandanātha. || 1.25 ||
Krodhānanda, Sukhānanda, and thereafter Jñānānanda; then Bodhānanda, and eternally the bliss of Kāraṇānanda. (1.26)
With rolling eyes and radiant with the touch of such power,
one should then satisfy them with a stream of honey-like nectar sparkling from the *bindu*.
Therefore, by that very same path, one should lead the supreme [deity] to her own abode;
O Goddess, one should contemplate oneself as pale-red due to the masses of her radiance. (1.28)
Thus, O Goddess, the unsurpassed morning rite has been told to you;
it must certainly be kept secret for my pleasure, O Sovereign of the Gods. (1.29)
Thus ends the first chapter in the glorious Tārā Tantra.
The Second Chapter.
Śrī Bhairavī said:
O highly fortunate one! I have heard this great morning ritual.
And in the tantra known as the Mahācīna, there is indeed a threefold worship. (2.1)
The Lord of Buddhas has spoken; there, the worship of the *yoni* was heard.
Now I desire to hear about the mental (*mānasa*) and the mechanical (*yāntrika*) forms of it. (2.2)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O beloved, I shall describe the procedure for mental worship; first, hear about the ritual placement (nyāsa).
For indeed, without the web of ritual consignments (nyāsa) being performed, there is no qualification [for practice]. (2.3)

The placement of the Ṛṣis and so forth, as well as the placement on the hands and limbs; the placement of the phonemes (varṇa) and the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-vinyāsa), followed by the placement of the sacred seat (pīṭha). (2.4)
Akṣobhya is declared to be the ṛṣi, the Vṛhatī meter is proclaimed, Ugratārā is said to be the deity, and the Kūrca seed-syllable is well-expounded. (2.5)
The power (śakti) is the weapon (astra), and the remaining letters become the pegs (kīlaka).
Having uttered [the mantra] in the form of the entirety of speech, one should say "Hṛdayāya namaḥ" (Salutation to the Heart).
Having uttered "Akhaṇḍavāgrūpiṇī" for the head, [one says] "Vahnivallabhā";
and having uttered "Brahmavāgrūpiṇī," one also says "Śikhāyai Vaṣaṭ."
Having uttered "Viṣṇuvāgrūpiṇī" for the armor (kavaca), this is declared;
likewise, "Viṣṇuvāgrūpiṇī netrattrayāya vauṣaṭ" is also [recited].
Having uttered [the mantra] "sarvavāgrūpiṇīm," one should recollect "astrāya phaṭ," and likewise utter the seed-syllables with the six long vowels and the *māyā* (ī) syllable. (2.9)
One should perform the placement of the fingers upon the limbs starting from the hands;
O Dear One, one should place [the mantras] beginning with the first letter and ending with the final letter upon the heart.

O Dear One! [Place] the consonants beginning with *e* and ending with *ṅ*, followed by those from *ḍha* to *na*, in sequence upon the pair of arms; then those from *ṇa* to *bha*, and from *ma* to *kṣa*, upon the two shanks. (2.11)
Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the root mantra, one should perform the placement of the seats (*pīṭha-nyāsa*).
Within the lotus of the heart is an ocean of nectar, and in its center is an island made of gold. (2.12)
On all sides were *pārijāta* trees, and in their midst stood the *kalpataru*;
at its base was a pavilion fashioned of gold, adorned with four doors.
Having established the ritual apparatus in that pavilion—which has been thoroughly perfumed and fanned by a gentle breeze—one should perform the worship there. (2.14)
Thus, one should contemplate Ugratāriṇī within the body composed of the sacred seats (pīṭha);
taking the tips of the fingers to the heart, one should perform the ritual placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa).
Thus, O beloved, I have told you this unsurpassed web of nyāsas;
O dear one, the sequence and the arrangement of these nyāsas must be learned from the Guru. (2.16)
Then one should perform worship by which one may attain identity with That;
and one should bathe in the pure sacred ford (tīrtha) of Puṣkara, which is situated within the heart.
The union of Śiva and Śakti is declared by the Tantrikas to be the *sandhyā*;
O beloved of Prāṇa, one should satisfy that [union] with the nectars flowing from the *bindu*. (2/18)
Then, having dissolved his sins, retinue, and so forth into that body, and having offered ointments and other services, one should bathe him with divine water. (2.19)
Having wiped [her] with a soft cloth, one should apply collyrium to the eyes,
vermilion to the forehead, and lac-dye to the lotus-feet.
One should mentally contemplate the form adorned with all ornaments;
then, meditating "I am He," one should offer water for the feet at the feet, O Dear One. (2.21)
One should sprinkle water worthy of honor upon the head, fragrance on the face, and [fragrance] everywhere on the limbs;
as well as fragrant substances, white and red flowers, the *javā* flower, and the black *aparājitā*.
One should place the garland upon the feet, the head, the ears, and the neck;
then, having offered incense and lamps before it, one should present the food offering.
Minced meat is the primary ingredient, and excellent fish is the next;
furthermore, one should provide roasted śāli rice as the final component. (2.24)
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should then cause liquor, followed by cakes and *śaṣkulī* sweets, to be offered;
then, having indeed presented liquor together with various side dishes (*temana*).
O Dear One! One should cause rice mixed with curd, milk, and ghee to be offered;
then one should give water for sipping (ācamana) and present betel leaf.
Then, having performed the mental recitation (*japa*), one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*);
having praised and bowed to the respective deities of the limbs, one should then cause [the deity] to depart.
Then, having sent the remainder [of the food] to their respective places, one should personally partake with the Śaktis.
Thereafter, one should meditate upon oneself as being identical with Tāriṇī, thinking "I am He (So'ham)."
O Goddess! This mental worship is said to be difficult to attain;
O Beloved, it consists of a mind that is singularly pure through the worship of the lotus of the heart. (2.29)
At the proper time for the worship of the Guru—whether in the morning or at midday—this should be performed according to the rules through the grace of the Guru’s feet. (2.30)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the worship as enjoined by the Yantra.
Then, having gone to the sacrificial hall, one should perform the gathering of flowers. (2.31)

Having uttered the word "śatābhiṣeka" twice, one should then recite: the *kūrca* mantra, the weapon (*astra*), fire (*vahni*), and the feminine (*lalanā*) mantras, preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ), for the drawing forth of flowers. (2.32)

Having first uttered *māyā* (hrlm), one should address the *ādhāraśakti*; then, for the worship of the seat, one should use the heart-mantra (*hṛnmanu*) ending in *ṅe* (namaḥ) directed toward the lotus-seated one (*kamalāsana*). (2.33)
Having placed the *arghya* vessel, one should perform the purification of the five;
O beloved, in the *Nīlatantra*, purification alone was taught at the very beginning. (2.34)
O Goddess! During the second purification, one should mutter the *pratadviṣṇu* mantra;
during the third purification, O Goddess, the knower of mantras should use the *tryambaka* mantra itself. (2.35)
One should perform the fourth purification with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," and the purification of the self-originated [liṅga] and others with the mantra "pra tad viṣṇuḥ. (2.36)
O beloved! Sexual intercourse is purified solely by the purification of the power (śakti).
Therefore, O Goddess, my dear, I shall now describe to you the great yantra. 2/37.
Then, O Goddess, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with sandalwood paste upon the *sayoni* [base], and then one should draw the square-shaped yantra with four gates. (2.38)
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa in the east, one should sacrifice to Vaṭuka in the south;
one should worship Kṣetrapāla in the west and Yoginī in the north. (2.39)
(9) There, the cremation ground (śmaśāna) is to be fully worshipped; there one should worship the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma).
At its root is a jeweled pedestal (maṇipīṭha), adorned with various gems. (2.40)
Richly adorned with various ornaments and graced by sages and gods, it was surrounded on all sides by auspicious female spirits who delighted in flesh and bones. (2.41)

Having uttered "Haḥ Sauḥ Sadāśiva," one should [visualize] corpses, skulls, funeral pyres, charcoal, and bones adorning the four directions; thereafter, [one addresses] the Great Preta. (In the four directions, adorned with corpses, skulls, funeral pyres, charcoal, and bones. 2/42.
The heart-mantra is prescribed for the lotus posture (padmāsana) during the ritual placement on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa):
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, and likewise Prīti. (2.43)
Fame, Peace, Nourishment, and Contentment—these are the eight powers (Śaktis).
O beloved of my life, these are to be worshipped in order upon the petals. (2.44)
Then, having offered a handful of flowers according to the principle of the Tortoise (Kūrmatattva),
the Kaulika [should contemplate] the radiant splendor within the heart, accompanied by its retinue.
O Goddess! One should place [the corpse] upon a shava with the syllable *yaṃ* as the beginning;
then, one should perform the ritual placement of the life-force (*jīvanyāsa*) with the mantra *āṃ so'haṃ*. (2.46)
Then, O Goddess, one should worship Ugratāriṇī with water for the feet and other offerings, using "Namaḥ," "Svāhā," "Svadhā," "Namo," and "Vauṣaṭ" in their respective order. (2.47)
Then, saying "I offer this," one should give everything, O Maheśvarī!
Having thus declared, "This is the substance," one should then perform the awakening of the deity.
p. 10) For each individual vajra-flower, one should say: *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Then, having uttered the root mantra, one should append the name ending in *-ṅ*. (2.49)
Then, O Goddess, the bow-maker (kauntika) should worship the retinues, reciting "This substance" followed by "Salutation to the retinues" at the end. (2.50)
A person of noble lineage should perform the worship with the mantra beginning with the *praṇava*;
he should place Akṣobhya at the crown of the head and [the other deities] on the eight petals starting from the east.
One should worship the eight Śaktis and the four Bhairavas at the gates, from the northwest (Vāyavya) to the northeast (Īśa), and the lineage of Gurus is established [therein]. (2.52)
Then, having recited [the mantra], praised with hymns, and bowed down, one should dissolve [the deity] into the heart;
and one should give the food offering to the practitioners and to women, but never [consume it] elsewhere.
Thus, O blessed lady, I have described to you the great worship of Tārā, which is traditionally taught as being both mental and mechanical, performed daily by men. (2.54)
O Goddess! Women have no authority over the mental or mechanical [forms of worship]. They must perform the worship as prescribed, or else they should not do it at their own will. (2.55)
Thus ends the second chapter in the glorious Tārā Tantra.
The third chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain; listen, O Daughter of the Mountain.
O beloved, [one may use] one bowl, or two, or three, or five. (3.1)
He who is the most excellent among the best of heroes drinks [it]; he is declared to be Rudra.
He who becomes the cause of this through the yoga of consciousness and bliss—[he is Rudra]. (3.2)
That alone is supreme bliss, which bestows union with Brahman;
therefore, having consumed the root of accomplishment, the practitioner should drink the cause.
That drinking of the cause which is devoid of bliss and consciousness does not produce bliss, just as the word of the Buddhist deity [teaches]. (3.4)
In this matter, the Guru is always to be honored, as is his son; likewise, his wife must always be honored with one's whole being by those who follow the Kaulika path. (3.5)
O beloved! By her mere satisfaction, the Goddess becomes pleased;
therefore, one should gratify the giver of Brahman with hymns, wealth, or words. (3.6)

O beloved, listen with a one-pointed mind to the procedure for the nocturnal recitation (*japa*): first, having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), then follow the meditation on the Guru. (3.7)
Thereafter, one should perform meditation on the mantra, and after that, meditation on the deity;
then, having recited the Tara-mantra which serves as a bridge, one should perform the recitation. (3.8)
Again, having performed the meditation on the Goddess with the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), one should offer [the self].
One should contemplate: "I am Śiva; my own self is the form of Tāriṇī. (3.9)
And one should meditate incessantly, thinking, "I am composed of my retinue.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this secret consisting of Tāriṇī. (3/10)
Therefore, an oath should not be given to a beast; such is my oath regarding you, my beloved!
Thus ends the third chapter in the venerable Tārā Tantra.
The Fourth Chapter.
The venerable Bhairavī said:
By whose grace this entire procedure for the practice of the Kula tradition [is revealed].
Now I desire to hear about the greatness of that very [place] from beginning to end. (4.1)
Śrī Bhairava said: The Guru, the Paramaguru, the Parāparaguru, and the Parameṣṭhiguru—these four are remembered as the Gurus. (4.2)
In this context, the *ṛṣi* is said to be the Guru; the giver of the mantra is the supreme Guru;
I am the Guru of the higher and the lower; and you alone are the *parameṣṭhin*. (4.3)
Among all of them, however, the supreme Guru is the most eminent;
without the Guru, neither Kāśī nor the Gaṅgā can grant great liberation. (4/4)
I shall declare its majesty, by which the consort of Śambhu is pleased;
the oneness of the Guru, the mantra, and the chosen deity is fully described. (4.5)
And his wife especially partakes in the excellence of the Supreme Goddess;
whether she be straightforward or crooked, or even harsh, she is one who speaks what is pleasing to her husband. (4.6)
O beloved, whether she is contemptible or diseased, ignorant or wise, she should be meditated upon by the best of the lineage as being identical with one's chosen deity. (4.7)

Whatever is spoken by one's own son, or whatever is uttered by the practitioner (sādhaka), should be carried out with great effort; even when it is impossible, one should remain diligent in the attempt.
The one who is beloved by heroes should, with a mind free of doubt, cause [the disciple] to eat the remains of the hero, the remains of wine, and likewise the remains of the spear-offering. (4.9)
O Bhairavī, listen to these five which were previously proclaimed, or even just one:
he who eats only after having purified and offered [the food] is indeed Bhairava. (4.10)
Those practitioners who are well-perfected and established in the sacred seats (pīṭha) are the basis for worship;
[this applies] to the Guru, his beloved wife, his sons, daughters, and the wives of practitioners. (4.11)
O Supreme Goddess, that which exists as effort and desire must be offered;
indeed, the worship of Śakti is ordained within the Tāriṇī mantra. (4.12)
One's own beloved wife should especially be worshipped as the chosen deity;
if she possesses a mantra identical to that of the deity, one should have her recite it. (4.13)
Then all purposes will be accomplished, for Tāriṇī becomes pleased;
since she is remembered as the beloved who constitutes half of his body, one should therefore be diligent in that regard. (4.14)
A brief account of her greatness has been declared by me in the Cīna-tantra;
here, the rule regarding those women who must be avoided during sexual union is stated. (4/15)

O Dear One! [The same applies to] the wife of the guru, the daughter of the guru, the son’s wife of the guru, as well as [the wives] of one who shares the same sacred site (satīrtha), of a hero (vīra), and of a practitioner (sādhaka). (4.16)
By sporting with a beloved woman who is a "mantra-daughter," one does not become a denizen of hell;
O Bhairavī, listen as the procedure for sexual union is now described. (4.17)

Having placed the Great Goddess beneath him and himself assuming the form of Bhairava, he should recite the root mantra before him while chanting the [mantra] beginning with "dharma-adharma" and so forth. (4.18)
One should unite the Bhairava of the Liṅga with the principle known as Gajatuṇḍa;
then, having recited [the mantra] one hundred or twenty times, one should cause the radiant energy (tejas) to descend.
Having recited the words "at the end of the root, however, one should manifest," thus it was told to you, O Goddess, exactly as spoken by the one whose form is the Buddha. 4/20
It bestows success through proper practice; it must be kept secret like one's own private parts. (4.21)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Tārā Tantra.
The Fifth Chapter.
The venerable Bhairavī said:
"O Mahādeva! By your grace, all of this has been understood by me."
Without the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), no fruit shall arise from the mantra.
And because it bestows the fruit [of practice], let the *puraścaraṇa* be explained.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme *puraścaraṇa*.
On a Tuesday or a Saturday, one should procure a human skull.
Having dug a pit measuring one *vitasti*, he who is free from attachment should bury it there;
for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra, he should recite it one thousand times during the night. (5.3)
By this very procedure, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is prescribed;
or else, the preliminary rite is described in another manner. (5.4)
O fair-faced one, having performed worship as if toward a deity for the guru, or his wife, or his son, or his daughter, one should perform japa until [the goal is attained]. 5/5.
Or else, one hundred and eight [recitations] are said to constitute the *puraścaraṇa*;
alternatively, having meditated upon [the deity] in the lotus of the head and performed worship, [one should proceed]. (5.6)
One who assumes the form of Bhairava should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times;
by this very procedure, it is called *puraścaraṇa*.
Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described:
beginning from the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] until the next fourteenth day. (5.8)
One should recite it one thousand and eight times every day; thus one becomes a master of supernatural powers (siddhi).
All of this is performed by heroes at night in a cremation ground.
Thus has this supreme *puraścaraṇa* been told to you, O blessed one!
It must be guarded with great effort, O beloved, just as a mother guards her secret from a lover.
Just as a living being deprived of life is incapable of performing any action, so too is a mantra declared to be ineffective when it is devoid of the *puraścaraṇa* rite. (5.11)
Whether once, twice, thrice, or even four times according to the distinction of the Yugas,
the supreme *puraścaraṇa* must be performed with diligent effort.
Now, O lady of excellent complexion, I shall describe the procedure for the offering of blood;
the blood of domestic, wild, and aquatic creatures increases one's devotion. (5.13)
O beloved of life! O daughter of the mountain! [One should offer] especially that which is smeared with ghee and honey, and filled with the blood of a living creature from a water-pot. (5.14)
Blood the size of a sesame seed from one's own body is recommended [to be applied] to the forehead, the hands, the heart, the head, and the area between the eyebrows. (5.15)
When his own blood has been given, he becomes like another body of Rudra—whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra. (5.16)
One should diligently offer one’s own blood after consecrating it with mantras;
however, women have no authority to offer the blood of their own bodies. (5.17)
I shall proclaim another mantra; listen with respect, O Bhairavī!
O Beloved, it consists of the three middle seed-syllables of the previously mentioned King of Mantras.
The goddess named Kulvukā and Mahānīlasarasvatī—indeed, there is only one Great Goddess who becomes threefold merely by name. (5.19)
Excluding the *praṇava*, there is a third [form] consisting of a single *jaṭā*;
just as the five-syllabled [mantra] becomes three syllables, so too does the four-syllabled [mantra]. (5.20)
"There is neither greatness nor division; it is called equality.
Thus, O beloved, this reality difficult to attain has been told by me to you. (5.21)
It should be guarded with great effort, just as one's own private parts are protected from another man. (5.22)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the venerable Tārā-tantra.
The Sixth Chapter.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now I shall further proclaim another secret concerning Tāriṇī.
I shall describe the majesty of the mantra of the triad beginning with Ugra.
Nevertheless, O Maheśvarī, I shall describe it here in brief:
the practitioner who knows the Tārā mantra, as well as the one who knows the Kālī mantra. (6.2)
O Goddess! He is even superior to Śiva; there should be no doubt in this matter.
O Goddess! [Without] the Tārā mantra, [there is nothing equal to] the Kālikā mantra itself.
O Supreme Goddess! one who knows the heart of Tāriṇī and is intent upon the practice of the creeper (latāsādhana) shall obtain enjoyment, liberation, fame, and prosperity. (6.4)
The wise one who performs the fifth consumption is honored even by the gods, both in his own form as a beloved wife and in his own form as a kinsman. (6/5)
(19) Through poverty, through opposition, through the infliction of insults and the like,
or through suffering and so forth, the gods may bring about a failure here in this practice.
Therefore, the lord of heroes should offer [the offering] to the Guru with effort;
for Tāriṇī is to be worshipped by all means and with every effort. (6.7)
"He who discriminates between the auspicious and the inauspicious is of dull intellect.
Thus has the reality been told to you in brief, and it should be put into practice. (6.8)
Those devotees of Śakti who enjoy happiness through vision [of the deity]—the Tārā-tantra, the Cīna-tantra, and the Kālī-tantra have been taught by the Guru. (6.9)
In every way, one should place the power upon the chest solely for the sake of concealment;
it should be given to a high-souled practitioner who is tranquil and wise.
O lady of excellent vows! [This applies] to the *vilāsinī*, the *svatantra*, and the *gurutantra*;
